replacement: As for the rest of life, with its so-called "experiences," which of us takes a serious enough interest in it? Or has enough time? I fear that in dealing with such matters we are never properly present: to be precise, our heart is not in it, and certainly not our ear. We are like a man lost in divine distraction, or sunk in the seas of his own soul, in whose ear the clock has just thundered its twelve strokes of noon with all its force. He suddenly wakes up and asks himself, "What in fact has just struck?" In the same way we sometimes rub our puzzled ears afterwards and ask, in complete astonishment and complete embarrassment, "What have we in fact just lived through?" And further, "Who are we in fact?" Then we count, after they have struck, as I have explained, all twelve throbbing beats of the clock of our experience, of our life, of our being — ah! — and we count wrong in the attempt. Of necessity we remain strangers to ourselves; we do not understand ourselves; we are bound to be mistaken about ourselves. For us the motto holds good for all eternity: "Each one is the farthest away from himself" — as far as ourselves are concerned, we are not "knowers."

When the aristocratic morality goes astray and commits sacrilege against reality, it does so only in the one sphere it does not know well enough — a sphere, in fact, whose real knowledge it disdainfully keeps away from. In some cases it misjudges the sphere it despises, that of the common, vulgar man and the low people. But we should also weigh this: the mood of contempt, of disdain, of superciliousness, even if it falsely portrays the object of its contempt, will always be far from the degree of falsity that marks the attacks — in effigy, of course — which the vindictive hatred and revengefulness of the weak launch against their enemies. In fact, contempt contains too strong a mixture of nonchalance, of casualness, of boredom, of impatience, even of personal exultation, to be able to distort its victim into a real caricature or a real monstrosity. Notice again the almost benevolent shades of meaning which, for instance, the Greek nobility puts into all the words by which it distinguishes the common people from itself. See how a kind of pity, care, and consideration keeps lending them a honeyed flavor, until at last almost all the words applied to the vulgar man survive as expressions for "unhappy," "worthy of pity" (compare δειλο, δείλαιος, πονηρός, μοχθηρός]; the last two really name the vulgar man as labor-slave and beast of burden) — and see how, conversely, "bad," "low," "unhappy" have never stopped ringing in the Greek ear with a tone in which "unhappy" is the dominant note. This is a heritage of the old noble aristocratic morality, which stays true to itself even in contempt (let philologists remember the sense in which ὀιζυρός, ἄνολβος, τλήμων, δυστυχεῑν, ξυμφορά used to be employed). The "well-born" simply felt themselves to be the "happy"; they did not have to manufacture their happiness artificially by looking at their enemies, or, when need arose, talk and lie themselves into happiness (as all resentful men are accustomed to do). And being complete men, exuberant with strength and therefore necessarily energetic, they were too wise to separate happiness from action: for them activity necessarily counts as happiness (that is the etymology of εὖ πρἆττειν). All this stands in sharp contrast to the "happiness" of the weak and the oppressed, with their festering venom and malignity, among whom happiness appears essentially as a narcotic, a deadening, a quietude, a peace, a "Sabbath," a slackening of the mind and a relaxation of the limbs — in short, as a purely passive phenomenon. The aristocratic man lived in confidence and openness with himself (gennaios, "noble-born," stresses the shade of meaning "sincere," and perhaps also "naïf"). The resentful man, on the other hand, is neither sincere nor naïf, nor honest and candid with himself. His soul squints; his mind loves hidden crannies, tortuous paths and back-doors; everything secret appeals to him as his world, his safety, his balm. He is a past master in silence, in not forgetting, in waiting, in provisional self-depreciation and self-abasement. A race of such resentful men will necessarily end up more prudent than any aristocratic race. It will honor prudence on quite a different scale, as a paramount condition of existence. Among aristocratic men, by contrast, prudence tends to carry a delicate flavor of luxury and refinement; so it plays nothing like so essential a part among them as the complete certainty with which the governing unconscious instincts function, or even a certain lack of prudence, such as a vehement and valiant charge against danger or the enemy, or those ecstatic bursts of rage, love, reverence, and gratitude by which noble souls have at all times recognized each other. When the resentment of the aristocratic man shows itself, it fulfills and exhausts itself in an immediate reaction, and so it instills no venom. On the other hand, in countless cases it never shows itself at all, where in the feeble and weak it would be inevitable. An inability to take their enemies, their disasters, their misdeeds seriously for any length of time — that is the sign of the full, strong natures who possess a superfluity of molding, plastic force that heals completely and produces forgetfulness. A good example of this in the modern world is Mirabeau, who had no memory for the insults and meannesses practiced on him, and who could not forgive only because he forgot. Such a man shakes off with a shrug many a worm which would have buried itself in another; only in characters like these do we see the possibility (supposing, of course, that there is such a possibility in the world) of the real "love of one's enemies." How much respect for his enemies, forsooth, is found in an aristocratic man — and such reverence is already a bridge to love! He insists on having his enemy to himself as his distinction. He tolerates no enemy except one in whose character there is nothing to despise and much to honor! Now imagine, on the other hand, the "enemy" as the resentful man conceives him — and it is exactly here that we see his work, his creativeness. He has conceived "the evil enemy," the "evil one," and that is the root idea from which he then derives, as a contrasting and corresponding figure, a "good one": himself — his very self!

11. This man's method is the exact opposite of the aristocrat's. The aristocrat forms the root idea "good" spontaneously, straight out of himself, and only then, from that material, creates for himself a concept of "bad"! This aristocratic "bad" and that "evil" from the cauldron of unsatisfied hatred are two very different things. The first is an imitation, an "extra," an additional nuance; the second is the original, the beginning, the essential act in the making of a slave-morality. Both "bad" and "evil" have the same opposite, "good," yet how great a difference they mark! For the idea "good" is not the same in each. Ask rather: "Who is really evil, according to the morality of resentment?" The answer, in all sternness, is this: just the good man of the other morality, just the aristocrat, the powerful one, the ruler, but seen through the venomous eye of resentfulness and so given a new color, a new meaning, a new look. We would be the last to deny this. A man who got to know those "good" ones only as enemies learned at the same time not to know them only as "evil enemies." Yet these same men are bound so rigorously inter pares by convention, respect, custom, and gratitude, and still more by mutual vigilance and jealousy inter pares. Among themselves they find so many new ways of showing consideration, self-control, delicacy, loyalty, pride, and friendship. But toward whatever lies outside their circle (where the foreign element, a foreign country, begins) they are not much better than beasts of prey let loose. There they are free of all social control. In the wilderness they can vent, with impunity, the tension built up by being fenced in and shut up within the peace of society. They revert to the innocence of the beast-of-prey conscience, like jubilant monsters who may be coming from a ghastly bout of murder, arson, rape, and torture, with bravado and moral equanimity, as if it were merely some wild student's prank, fully convinced that the poets now have plenty to sing and celebrate. At the core of all these aristocratic races we cannot fail to recognize the beast of prey, the magnificent blond brute, greedily prowling for spoil and victory. This hidden core needed an outlet from time to time; the beast had to get loose again and return to the wilderness. The Roman, Arabic, German, and Japanese nobility, the Homeric heroes, the Scandinavian Vikings, all share this need. The aristocratic races left the idea "Barbarian" behind on every path they marched. Nay, a consciousness of this very barbarianism, and even a pride in it, shows itself in their highest civilization (for example, when Pericles tells his Athenians in the celebrated funeral oration, "Our audacity has forced a way over every land and sea, rearing everywhere imperishable memorials of itself for good and for evil"). The audacity of aristocratic races may be mad, absurd, and spasmodic in its expression; their enterprises may be incalculable and fantastic — Pericles sets in special relief and glory the ᾽ραθυμία of the Athenians, their nonchalance and contempt for safety, body, life, and comfort, their awful joy and intense delight in all destruction, in all the ecstasies of victory and cruelty — all these features crystallized, for those who suffered from them, into the picture of the "barbarian," of the "evil enemy," perhaps of the "Goth" and the "Vandal." Even now, the German meets a profound, icy mistrust as soon as he comes to power. That mistrust is still an aftermath of the inextinguishable horror with which Europe, for whole centuries, regarded the wrath of the blond Teuton beast (although there is scarcely a psychological, let alone a physical, relationship between the old Germans and ourselves). I once pointed out Hesiod's embarrassment when he conceived the series of social ages and tried to express them in gold, silver, and bronze. The Homeric world confronted him with a contradiction: an age magnificent indeed, but at the same time so awful and so violent. He could resolve it only by making two ages out of one and setting them one behind the other. First came the age of the heroes and demigods, as that world lived on in the memories of the aristocratic families, who found their own ancestors in it. Then came the bronze age, as that same age looked to the descendants of the oppressed, spoiled, ill-treated, exiled, and enslaved: an age of bronze, as I have said, hard, cold, terrible, without feelings and without conscience, crushing everything and spattering everything with blood. Suppose the now-accepted theory is true, that the whole essence of civilization is to train the beast of prey out of man and make of him a tame and civilized animal, a domesticated animal. Then we must undoubtedly regard as the real tools of civilization all those instincts of reaction and resentment, with whose help the aristocratic races, together with their ideals, were finally degraded and overpowered. That is not yet to say that the bearers of those tools also represented civilization. The opposite is not merely probable — nay, it is palpable today. These bearers of vindictive instincts that have to be bottled up, these descendants of all European and non-European slavery, especially of the pre-Aryan population — these people, I say, represent the decline of humanity! These "tools of civilization" are a disgrace to humanity, and in reality they count more as an argument against civilization, more as a reason to be suspicious of it. One may be quite justified in always fearing the blond beast at the core of every aristocratic race, and in staying on one's guard. But who would not a hundred times rather fear, while admiring, than be free of fear and be forever obsessed with the loathsome sight of the distorted, the dwarfed, the stunted, the envenomed? And is that not our fate? What makes us feel repulsion toward "man" today? — for we suffer from "man," there is no doubt about it. It is not fear. It is rather that we have nothing left to fear from men; that the worm "man" is in the foreground and swarms; that the "tame man," the wretched, mediocre, unedifying creature, has learned to consider himself a goal and a pinnacle, an inner meaning, a historic principle, a "higher man." Yes, and he has a certain right to do so, in so far as he feels that, set against that excess of deformity, disease, exhaustion, and effeteness whose odor is beginning to pollute present-day Europe, he at any rate has achieved a relative success; he at any rate still says "yes" to life.

15. In the faith in what? In the love for what? In the hope of what? These weaklings! — they also, forsooth, wish to be the strong some time; there is no doubt about it, some time their kingdom also must come — "the kingdom of God" is their name for it, as has been mentioned: they are so meek in everything! Yet to experience that kingdom one has to live long, to live beyond death — yes, eternal life is necessary, so that one can make up forever for that earthly life "in faith," "in love," "in hope." Make up for what? Make up by what? Dante, it seems to me, made a crass mistake when, with awe-inspiring ingenuity, he placed the inscription "Me too made eternal love" over the gate of his hell. At any rate, the inscription "Me too made eternal hate" would have a much better right to stand over the gate of the Christian Paradise and its "eternal blessedness" — granted, of course, that a truth may rightly stand over the gate to a lie! For what is the blessedness of that Paradise? Possibly we could quickly guess it; but it is better to have it explicitly attested by an authority not to be disparaged in such matters, Thomas of Aquinas, the great teacher and saint. "Beati in regno celesti" he says, as gently as a lamb, "videbunt pœnas damnatorum, ut beatitudo illis magis complaceat." Or if we wish to hear a stronger tone, here is a word from the mouth of a triumphant father of the Church, who warned his disciples against the cruel ecstasies of the public spectacles — But why? Faith offers us much more, he says, de Spectac., c. 29 ss., something much stronger. Thanks to the redemption, joys of quite another kind are at our disposal; instead of athletes we have our martyrs; if we wish for blood, well, we have the blood of Christ — but what then awaits us on the day of his return, of his triumph. And then he goes on, this enraptured visionary: "at enim supersunt alia spectacula, ille ultimas et perpetuus judicii dies, ille nationibus insperatus, ille derisus, cum tanta sæculi vetustas et tot ejus nativitates uno igne haurientur. Quæ tunc spectaculi latitudo! Quid admirer! quid rideam! Ubigaudeam! Ubi exultem, spectans tot et tantos reges, qui in cœlum recepti nuntiabantur, cum ipso Jove et ipsis suis testibus in imis tenebris congemescentes! Item præsides" (the provincial governors) "persecutores dominici nominis sævioribus quam ipsi flammis sævierunt insultantibus contra Christianos liquescentes! Quos præterea sapientes illos philosophos coram discipulis suis una conflagrantibus erubescentes, quibus nihil ad deum pertinere suadebant, quibus animas aut nullas aut non in pristina corpora redituras affirmabant! Etiam poetas non ad Rhadamanti nec ad Minois, sed ad inopinati Christi tribunal palpitantes! Tunc magis tragœdi audiendi, magis scilicet vocales" (with louder tones and more violent shrieks) "in sua propria calamitate; tunc histriones cognoscendi, solutiores multo per ignem; tunc spectandus auriga in flammea rota totus rubens, tunc xystici contemplandi non in gymnasiis, sed in igne jaculati, nisi quod ne tunc quidem illos velim vivos, ut qui malim ad eos potius conspectum insatiabilem conferre, qui in dominum scevierunt. Hic est ille, dicam fabri aut quæstuariæ filius" (as the whole of the following shows, and in particular this well-known description of the mother of Jesus from the Talmud, Tertullian is from here on referring to the Jews), "sabbati destructor, Samarites et dæmonium habens. Hic est quem a Juda redemistis, hic est ille arundine et colaphis diverberatus, sputamentis de decoratus, felle et acete potatus. Hic est, quem clam discentes subripuerunt, ut resurrexisse dicatur vel hortulanus detraxit, ne lactucæ suæ frequentia commeantium laderentur. Ut talia species, ut talibus exultes, quis tibi prætor aut consul aut sacerdos de sua liberalitate prastabit? Et tamen hæc jam habemus quodammodo per fidem spiritu imaginante repræsentata. Ceterum qualia illa sunt, quæ nec oculus vidit nec auris audivit nec in cor hominis ascenderunt?" (I Cor. ii. 9.) "Credo circo et utraque cavea" (the first and fourth row, or, according to others, the comic and the tragic stage) "et omni studio gratiora." Per fidem: so it stands written.

Which of them has been victorious for the time being, Rome or Judæa? There is not a shadow of doubt. Just consider whom you bow down to even in Rome itself today, as though to the quintessence of all the highest values — and not only in Rome, but over almost half the world, wherever man has been tamed or is about to be tamed. You bow to three Jews, as we know, and one Jewess (Jesus of Nazareth, Peter the fisher, Paul the tent-maker, and the mother of the aforesaid Jesus, named Mary). This is very remarkable: Rome is undoubtedly defeated. At any rate, in the Renaissance there was a brilliantly sinister revival of the classical ideal, of the aristocratic valuation of all things. Rome herself, like a man waking from a trance, stirred under the weight of the new Judaized Rome built over her, which looked like an œcumenical synagogue and was called the "Church." But Judæa immediately triumphed again, thanks to that fundamentally popular (German and English) movement of revenge called the Reformation, and thanks also to its inevitable corollary, the restoration of the Church — which also restored the ancient graveyard peace of classical Rome. In the French Revolution Judæa again proved victorious over the classical ideal, in a sense even more crucial and more profound. The last political aristocracy in Europe, that of seventeenth- and eighteenth-century France, broke into pieces under the instincts of a resentful populace. The world had never heard a greater jubilation, a more uproarious enthusiasm. Yet in the midst of it the most monstrous and unexpected thing happened: the ancient ideal itself rose before the eyes and conscience of humanity with all its life and with unheard-of splendor. Against resentment's lying war-cry of the prerogative of the most, against the will to lowliness, abasement, and equalization, the will to a retrogression and twilight of humanity, there rang out once more, stronger, simpler, and more penetrating than ever, the terrible and enchanting counter-warcry of the prerogative of the few! Then, like a final signpost to other ways, Napoleon appeared, the most unique and violent anachronism that ever existed, and in him the incarnate problem of the aristocratic ideal in itself. Consider well what a problem it is: Napoleon, that synthesis of Monster and Superman.

Note. — This treatise gives me the opportunity to express, openly and formally, a wish I have so far voiced only in occasional conversations with scholars. I wish that some Faculty of philosophy would earn the glory of promoting further study of the history of morals through a series of prize essays; perhaps this book may give a forceful impetus in that direction. For such a possibility, the following question deserves consideration. It deserves the attention of philologists and historians quite as much as that of actual professional philosophers.

1. Breeding an animal that can make promises — is this not the very paradox of a task that nature has set itself with regard to man? Is it not the real problem of man? Anyone who can fully appreciate the force of forgetfulness, which works against it, will find it all the more remarkable that the problem has been largely solved. Forgetfulness is not simply a vis inertiæ, as the superficial believe. It is rather an active power of obstruction, positive in the strictest sense of the word. It is the reason why nothing we live through, experience or take into ourselves enters consciousness while we digest it (we might call this psychic absorption), any more than the whole manifold process of our physical nutrition, the so-called "incorporation," does. The doors and windows of consciousness are shut for a time. We are relieved of the clamor of alarms and skirmishes with which our subconscious world of servant organs works in mutual co-operation and antagonism. There is a little quiet, a little tabula rasa of consciousness, to make room again for the new, and above all for the nobler functions and functionaries: room for government, foresight, predetermination (for our organism is built on an oligarchic model). This, as I have said, is the use of active forgetfulness. It is a very sentinel and nurse of psychic order, repose and etiquette; and it shows at once why there can be no happiness, no gladness, no hope, no pride, no real present, without forgetfulness. If this preventive apparatus is damaged and broken in a man, he is like a dyspeptic, and more than like one — he can "get rid of" nothing. But this very animal, who must be forgetful, and in whom forgetfulness is a force and a form of robust health, has bred for himself an opposing power, a memory, with whose help forgetfulness is in certain cases held in check — namely in the cases where promises have to be made. So this memory is by no means a merely passive inability to get rid of an impression once made, nor merely the indigestion caused by a pledged word that one cannot dispose of. It is an active refusal to get rid of it, a continuing and a wish to continue what was once willed: an actual memory of the will. Between the original "I will," "I shall do," and the actual discharge of the will, its act, we can therefore easily interpose a world of new and strange circumstances, events and even acts of will, without snapping this long chain of the will. But what does all this presuppose? In order to regulate the future in this way, man must first have learnt, and learnt thoroughly, to distinguish necessitated from accidental events, to think causally, to see the distant as present and anticipate it, to fix with certainty what is the end and what the means to that end, and above all to reckon, to be able to calculate. Man must first have become thoroughly calculable, disciplined, necessitated, even in his own eyes and his own conception of himself, so that, like a man making a promise, he could guarantee himself as a future.

2. All this is simply the long history of the origin of responsibility. The task of breeding an animal that can make promises includes, as we have already seen, a more immediate task as its condition and preliminary: first to make man to a certain extent necessitated, uniform, like among his like, regular and therefore calculable. What I have called the "morality of custom" (cp. Dawn of Day, Aphs. 9, 14, and 16) was an immense work: man's actual work on himself during the longest period of the human race, his whole prehistoric work. This work finds its meaning and its great justification (in spite of all its innate hardness, despotism, stupidity and idiocy) in this: with the help of the morality of customs and of social strait-waistcoats, man was made genuinely calculable. But suppose we stand at the end of this colossal process, at the point where the tree finally ripens its fruit and society and its morality of custom at last bring to light what they were only the means to. There we find, as the ripest fruit on its tree, the sovereign individual, who resembles only himself, who has got loose from the morality of custom: the autonomous "super-moral" individual (for "autonomous" and "moral" exclude each other) — in short, the man of the personal, long and independent will, who is able to promise. In him we find a proud consciousness, vibrating in every fibre, of what has at last been achieved and has come alive in him, a genuine consciousness of power and freedom, a feeling of human perfection in general. And this man who has grown to freedom, who is really able to promise, this lord of the free will, this sovereign — how can he fail to know how great his superiority is over everything that cannot bind itself by promises or be its own security, how great a trust, awe and reverence he awakens (he "deserves" all three), and that with this mastery over himself he is necessarily also given mastery over circumstances, over nature, over all creatures with shorter wills and less reliable characters? The "free" man, the owner of a long, unbreakable will, finds in this possession his standard of value. Looking out from himself upon others, he honors or he despises. Just as necessarily as he honors his peers, the strong and the reliable (those who can bind themselves by promises) — that is, everyone who promises like a sovereign, with difficulty, rarely and slowly, who is sparing with his trust but confers honor by the very act of trusting, who gives his word as something that can be relied on because he knows himself strong enough to keep it even in the teeth of disasters, even in the "teeth of fate" — so with equal necessity will he have the heel of his foot ready for the lean and empty jackasses who promise when they have no business to, and his rod of chastisement ready for the liar who already breaks his word at the very moment it is on his lips. The proud knowledge of the extraordinary privilege of responsibility, the consciousness of this rare freedom, of this power over himself and over fate, has sunk right down to his innermost depths and has become an instinct, a dominating instinct. What name will he give to it, to this dominating instinct, if he needs a word for it? There is no doubt about it: the sovereign man calls it his conscience.

3. His conscience? — One sees at once that the idea "conscience," which appears here in its supreme form, supreme almost to the point of strangeness, must already have a long history and evolution behind it. To be able to guarantee oneself with all due pride, and at the same time to say yes to oneself — that is, as has been said, a ripe fruit, but also a late fruit. How long this fruit had to hang sour and bitter on the tree! And for a still longer period there was not a glimpse of such a fruit to be had. No one had taken it on himself to promise it, although everything on the tree was quite ready for it and everything was maturing toward that very consummation. "How is a memory to be made for the man-animal? How is an impression to be fixed so deeply upon this ephemeral understanding, half dense and half silly, upon this incarnate forgetfulness, that it will stay permanently present?" One may imagine that this primeval problem was not solved with exactly gentle answers and gentle means. Perhaps there is nothing more awful and more sinister in the early history of man than his system of mnemonics. "Something is burnt in so that it stays in his memory: only what never stops hurting stays in his memory." This is an axiom of the oldest (unfortunately also the longest) psychology in the world. It might even be said that wherever solemnity, seriousness, mystery and gloomy colors are now found in the life of men and nations, there is some survival of that horror which was once the universal companion of all promises, pledges and obligations. The past, the past with all its length, depth and hardness, breathes on us and wells up in us again when we become "serious." Whenever man has thought it necessary to make a memory for himself, it has never happened without blood, tortures and sacrifice. The most dreadful sacrifices and forfeitures belong here (among them the sacrifice of the first-born), the most loathsome mutilations (for instance, castration), the most cruel rituals of all the religious cults (for all religions are really at bottom systems of cruelty) — all these things originate in that instinct which found in pain its most potent mnemonic. In a certain sense the whole of asceticism is to be ascribed to this. Certain ideas have to be made inextinguishable, omnipresent, "fixed," with the aim of hypnotizing the whole nervous and intellectual system through these "fixed ideas" — and the ascetic methods and modes of life are the means of freeing those ideas from competition with all other ideas, so as to make them "unforgettable." The worse man's memory was, the ghastlier the signs presented by his customs. The severity of the penal laws in particular gives a gauge of how hard man found it to conquer forgetfulness, and to keep a few primal postulates of social life present in the minds of those who were slaves of every momentary emotion and every momentary desire. We Germans certainly do not regard ourselves as an especially cruel and hard-hearted nation, still less as an especially casual and happy-go-lucky one. But one has only to look at our old penal ordinances to realize how much trouble it takes in the world to develop a "nation of thinkers" (I mean: the European nation that today shows the maximum of reliability, seriousness, bad taste and positiveness, and that on the strength of these qualities has a right to train every kind of European mandarin). These Germans used terrible means to make a memory for themselves, to master their rooted plebeian instincts and the brutal crudity of those instincts. Think of the old German punishments: stoning (as far back as the legend, the millstone falls on the head of the guilty man); breaking on the wheel (the most original invention and speciality of the German genius in the sphere of punishment); dart-throwing; tearing or trampling by horses ("quartering"); boiling the criminal in oil or wine (still practiced in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries); the highly popular flaying ("slicing into strips"); cutting the flesh out of the breast. Think also of the evil-doer smeared with honey and then exposed to the flies in a blazing sun. With the help of such images and precedents man finally kept in his memory five or six "I will nots," about which he had already given his promise so as to enjoy the advantages of society — and truly, with the help of this kind of memory man finally arrived at "reason"! Alas! Reason, seriousness, mastery over the emotions, all these gloomy, dismal things called reflection, all these privileges and pageantries of humanity: how dear is the price they have exacted! How much blood and cruelty lies at the foundation of all "good things"!

Have these current genealogists of morals ever allowed themselves even the vaguest notion, for instance, that the cardinal moral idea of "ought" originates in the very material idea of "owe"? Or that punishment developed as a retaliation absolutely independently of any prior assumption about the freedom or determination of the will? — And this to such an extent that a high degree of civilization was always necessary first, before the animal man could begin to make those much more primitive distinctions of "intentional," "negligent," "accidental," "responsible," and their contraries, and apply them in assessing punishment. That idea — "the wrong-doer deserves punishment because he might have acted otherwise" — is nowadays so cheap, obvious, natural and inevitable, and has had to serve as an illustration of how the sentiment of justice appeared on earth; yet in fact it is an exceedingly late, even refined, form of human judgment and inference, and to project it back to the beginning of the world is simply a clumsy violation of the principles of primitive psychology. Throughout the longest period of human history punishment was never based on the evil-doer's responsibility for his action, and was therefore not based on the assumption that only the guilty should be punished. On the contrary, punishment was inflicted for the same reason that parents punish their children even nowadays: out of anger at an injury suffered, an anger that vents itself mechanically on the author of the injury. But this anger is kept in bounds and modified by the idea that every injury has somewhere its equivalent price and can really be paid off, even if by means of pain to the author. Where has this ancient, deep-rooted and now perhaps ineradicable idea, the idea of an equivalence between injury and pain, drawn its strength? I have already revealed its origin: it lies in the contractual relationship between creditor and debtor, which is as old as the existence of legal rights at all, and which in its turn points back to the primary forms of purchase, sale, barter and trade.

5. The realization of these contractual relations naturally arouses (as our previous remarks would lead us to expect) a great deal of suspicion and opposition toward the primitive society that made or sanctioned them. In this society promises will be made; in this society the aim is to give the promiser a memory; in this society, as we may suspect, there will be full scope for hardness, cruelty and pain. The "debtor," in order to inspire credit in his promise of repayment, in order to guarantee the earnestness and sanctity of his promise, in order to drill into his own conscience the duty, the solemn duty, of repayment, will pledge something he still possesses, something still in his power, under a contract with his creditor to cover the case of his not paying. He may pledge his life or his wife, or his freedom or his body (or, under certain religious conditions, even his salvation, his soul's welfare, even his peace in the grave; so in Egypt, where the corpse of the debtor found no rest from the creditor even in the grave — and from the Egyptian standpoint this peace was of particular importance). But above all the creditor has the power to inflict on the body of the debtor all kinds of pain and torture, for instance to cut off as much as seemed proportionate to the size of the debt. From this point of view precise schemes of valuation arose early and everywhere, often horrible in the minuteness and meticulousness with which they were applied: legally sanctioned valuations for individual limbs and parts of the body. I consider it already a progress, a proof of a freer, less petty and more Roman conception of law, when the Roman Code of the Twelve Tables decreed that it did not matter how much or how little the creditors cut off in such a case: "si plus minusve secuerunt, ne fraude esto." Let us make the logic of this whole process of equalization clear; it is strange enough. The equivalence is this: instead of an advantage that directly compensates for his injury (that is, instead of an equalization in money, lands or some kind of chattel), the creditor is granted, by way of repayment and compensation, a certain sensation of satisfaction. It is the satisfaction of being able to vent his power without any trouble on one who is powerless, the delight "de faire le mal pour le plaisir de le faire," the joy in sheer violence. This joy will be relished in proportion to the lowness and humbleness of the creditor's place in society, and it is quite apt to have the effect of the most delicious dainty, and even to seem a foretaste of a higher social position. Thanks to the punishment of the "debtor," the creditor shares in the rights of the masters. At last he too, for once, attains the edifying consciousness of being able to despise and ill-treat a creature as an "inferior" — or at any rate of seeing him despised and ill-treated, in case the actual power of punishing, the administration of punishment, has already been transferred to the "authorities." So the compensation consists in a claim on cruelty and a right to draw on it.

7. Since I hold these thoughts, I am, let me say in parenthesis, fundamentally opposed to supplying our pessimists with fresh water for the discordant, groaning mills of their disgust with life. On the contrary, it should be shown specifically that at the time when mankind was not yet ashamed of its cruelty, life on earth was brighter than it is nowadays, when there are pessimists. The darkening of the heavens over man has always grown in proportion to the growth of man's shame before man. The tired pessimistic outlook, the mistrust of the riddle of life, the icy negation of disgusted ennui — none of these is a sign of the most evil age of the human race. Much rather do they first come to light, as the swamp-flowers they are, when the swamp they belong to comes into existence. I mean the diseased refinement and moralization thanks to which the "animal man" has at last learnt to be ashamed of all his instincts. On the road to angelhood (not to use a harder word in this context) man has developed that dyspeptic stomach and coated tongue which have made not only the joy and innocence of the animal repulsive to him, but life itself — so that sometimes he stands before his own self with stopped nostrils and, like Pope Innocent the Third, draws up a black list of his own horrors ("unclean generation, loathsome nutrition when in the maternal body, badness of the matter out of which man develops, awful stench, secretion of saliva, urine, and excrement"). Nowadays suffering is always trotted out as the first argument against existence, as its most sinister question. It is well, then, to remember the times when men judged on the opposite principle because they could not do without inflicting suffering, and saw in it a magic of the first order, a veritable bait of seduction to life.

11. I must say a discouraging word here about the recent attempts to base the origin of justice on something quite different, namely resentment. Let me whisper in the psychologists' ear, if they want to study revenge itself up close: this plant flourishes loveliest today among Anarchists and anti-Semites. It is a hidden flower, as it has always been, like the violet, though, to be sure, with another perfume. Like must come from like, so we should not be surprised to find in just such circles the birth of efforts (it is their old birthplace; compare above, First Essay, paragraph 14) to sanctify revenge under the name of justice, as though Justice were at bottom only a development of the consciousness of injury. By rehabilitating revenge in this way, they hope to reinstate all the reactive emotions generally and collectively. That last point is the one I object to least. Seen from the standpoint of the whole problem of biology (from which the value of these emotions has until now been underestimated), it even seems meritorious. What I alone want to point out is that this new nuance of scientific equity (which works for the benefit of hate, envy, mistrust, jealousy, suspicion, rancor, revenge) grows out of the spirit of revenge itself. This scientific "equity" breaks off at once, and makes way for the accents of deadly enmity and prejudice, whenever another group of emotions appears. In my opinion these emotions have a much higher biological value than the reactions, and so have a paramount claim to the valuation and appreciation of science: I mean the really active emotions, such as personal and material ambition, and so forth. (E. Dühring, Value of Life; Course of Philosophy, and passim.) That is enough against this tendency in general. As for Dühring's particular maxim, that the home of Justice lies in the sphere of the reactive feelings, our love of truth forces us to turn his own proposition sharply around and set against it this other: the last sphere conquered by the spirit of justice is the sphere of the feeling of reaction! Suppose the just man really stays just even toward the person who injures him (and is not merely cold, moderate, reserved, indifferent: being just is always a positive state). Suppose that, despite the strong provocation of personal insult, contempt and calumny, the lofty, clear objectivity of the just and judging eye (whose glance is as profound as it is gentle) remains untroubled. Why, then we have a piece of perfection, a past master of the world; but it would not be wise to expect such a thing, and at any rate it should not be too easily believed. Speaking generally, there is no doubt that even the justest individual needs only a small dose of hostility, malice or innuendo to send the blood to his head and drive the fairness out. The active, attacking, aggressive man is always a hundred degrees nearer to justice than the man who merely reacts. He certainly has no need to use the tactics the reacting man must use, of falsifying and biasing his valuation of his object. For this very reason the aggressive man has at all times had the stronger, bolder, more aristocratic and also freer outlook, and the better conscience. On the other hand, we already suspect who has the invention of the "bad conscience" on his own conscience: the resentful man! Finally, let man look at himself in history. Where has the whole administration of law, the real need of law, had its earthly home until now? Perhaps with the reacting man? Not for a minute. Rather with the active, strong, spontaneous, aggressive man? I deliberately defy the agitator I mentioned (who himself makes this self-confession, "the creed of revenge has run through all my works and endeavors like the red thread of Justice"), and I say that, judged historically, law on earth is the very war against the reactive feelings. It is a war waged on them by the powers of activity and aggression, which spend part of their strength on damming and holding within bounds this effervescence of hysterical reactivity, and on forcing it into some compromise. Wherever justice is practiced and maintained, we can see the stronger power looking for weapons to end the senseless fury of resentment among the weaker powers beneath it (whether groups or individuals). It does this partly by pulling the victim of resentment out of the clutches of revenge, partly by putting a campaign of its own against the enemies of peace and order in the place of revenge, partly by finding, suggesting and sometimes enforcing settlements, and partly by fixing standard equivalents for injuries, to which resentment is from then on finally referred. The most drastic step the supreme power takes against the preponderance of spite and vindictiveness, and it takes it as soon as it is strong enough, is to found law: it declares imperatively what in its eyes counts as just and lawful and what as unjust and unlawful. Once law is founded, the supreme power treats the aggressive and arbitrary acts of individuals, or of whole groups, as violations of law and as revolt against itself. That draws its subjects' feelings away from the immediate injury such a violation causes, and so in the end it achieves the very opposite of what revenge always wants, since revenge sees and recognizes only the standpoint of the injured party. From then on the eye is trained toward an ever more impersonal valuation of the deed, even the eye of the injured party himself (though that comes last of all, as I remarked before). On this principle "right" and "wrong" first arise after the foundation of law (and not, as Dühring maintains, only after the act of violation). To speak of intrinsic right and intrinsic wrong is absolute nonsense. An injury, an oppression, an exploitation, an annihilation cannot be intrinsically wrong, because life is essentially (that is, in its cardinal functions) something that works by injuring, oppressing, exploiting and annihilating, and cannot be conceived at all without this character. I must make a still more serious confession. From the most advanced biological standpoint, conditions of legality can only be exceptional conditions. They are partial restrictions of the real life-will, which aims at power, and they are subordinate to that life-will's general end as particular means, that is, as means of creating larger units of strength. Imagine a legal organization conceived as sovereign and universal, not as a weapon in the fight between complexes of power but as a weapon against fighting, something in the style of Dühring's communistic model in which every will is treated as equal to every other will. It would be a principle hostile to life, a destroyer and dissolver of man, an outrage on the future of man, a symptom of fatigue, a secret path to Nothingness. —

13. Back to our subject, punishment. We must draw a double distinction. On one side is the relatively permanent element: the custom, the act, the "drama," a certain rigid sequence of procedures. On the other is the fluid element: the meaning, the end, the expectation that goes with carrying out such procedures. Here we at once assume, per analogiam (following the theory of the historical method developed above), that the procedure itself is older and earlier than its use for punishment. That use was introduced and read into the procedure (which had existed for a long time but was employed with another meaning). In short, the case is different from what our naïf genealogists of morals and of law have supposed until now. They thought the procedure was invented for the purpose of punishment, just as they had earlier thought the hand was invented for the purpose of grasping. Now the other element in punishment, the fluid one, its meaning. At a very late stage of civilization (for instance in contemporary Europe), the idea of punishment no longer shows just one meaning but a whole synthesis "of meanings." The past history of punishment in general, the history of its use for the most diverse ends, finally crystallizes into a kind of unity that is hard to break down into its parts, and that, it must be stressed, absolutely defies definition. (Today it is impossible to say definitely why people punish at all. Every idea in which a whole process is promiscuously summed up eludes definition; only what has no history can be defined.) At an earlier stage, on the contrary, that synthesis of meanings looks much less rigid and much more elastic. We can see how, in each individual case, the elements of the synthesis change their value and their position, so that now one element stands out and dominates the rest, now another; nay, in certain cases one element (perhaps the end of deterrence) seems to wipe out all the others. At any rate, to give some idea of how uncertain, supplementary and accidental the meaning of punishment is, and of how one identical procedure can be used and adapted for the most diametrically opposed objects, I will set down here a scheme that has suggested itself to me, itself based on comparatively small and accidental material. — Punishment as making the criminal harmless and unable to do further injury. — Punishment as compensation to the injured party for the injury sustained, in any form whatsoever (including the form of sentimental compensation). — Punishment as the isolation of whatever disturbs the equilibrium, in order to stop the disturbance from spreading further. — Punishment as a means of inspiring fear of those who determine and carry out the punishment. — Punishment as a kind of compensation for advantages the wrong-doer has enjoyed until then (for example, when he is put to work as a slave in the mines). — Punishment as the elimination of an element of decay (sometimes of a whole branch, as under the Chinese laws, and so as a means of purifying the race or preserving a social type). — Punishment as a festival, as the violent oppression and humiliation of an enemy who has at last been subdued. — Punishment as a mnemonic, whether for the man who suffers it (the so-called "correction") or for those who witness it being carried out. Punishment as the payment of a fee stipulated by the power that protects the evil-doer from the excesses of revenge. — Punishment as a compromise with the natural phenomenon of revenge, in so far as the stronger races still maintain revenge and claim it as a privilege. — Punishment as a declaration and measure of war against an enemy of peace, of law, of order, of authority. Society fights him with the weapons war provides, as a spirit dangerous to the community, as a breaker of the contract on which the community is based, as a rebel, a traitor and a breaker of the peace.

14. This list is certainly not complete; punishment, obviously, is overloaded with utilities of every kind. That makes it all the more permissible to remove one supposed utility, which passes, at any rate in the popular mind, for the most essential of all. It is just this utility that still gives the strongest support to the faith in punishment, a faith that is tottering today for many reasons. Punishment is supposed to be valuable because it awakens in the guilty the consciousness of guilt. In punishment people look for the proper instrumentum of that psychic reaction known as the "bad conscience," "remorse." But this theory violates reality and psychology even as applied to the present; how much worse when it is applied to the longest period of man's history, his primitive history! Genuine remorse is certainly extremely rare among wrong-doers and the victims of punishment. Prisons and houses of correction are not the soil in which this worm of remorse likes best to breed. All conscientious observers agree on this, and in many cases they reach such a judgment only reluctantly and against their own wishes. Generally speaking, punishment hardens and numbs, it concentrates, it sharpens the consciousness of alienation, it strengthens the power of resistance. Sometimes it breaks a man's energy and brings about a piteous prostration and abjectness. That result is certainly even less salutary than the average effect of punishment, which is a harsh and sinister doggedness. Thinking of those prehistoric millennia, we must conclude without hesitation that punishment, more than anything, held back the development of the consciousness of guilt, at any rate in the victims of the punishing power. In particular, let us not underestimate how far the sight of the judicial and executive procedure itself keeps the wrong-doer from feeling that his deed, the character of his act, is intrinsically reprehensible. He sees the same kind of acts clearly practiced in the service of justice, then called good, and practiced with a good conscience: espionage, trickery, bribery, trapping, the whole intriguing and insidious art of the policeman and the informer. He sees the whole system, in fact, that appears in the various kinds of punishment (a system excused not by passion but based on principle), of robbing, oppressing, insulting, imprisoning, racking, murdering. And he sees his judges treat all this not as acts deserving censure and condemnation in themselves, but only in a particular context and application. The "bad conscience," that most sinister and interesting plant of our earthly vegetation, did not grow in this soil. In fact, for a very long period, the man who judged and punished had no idea at all that he was dealing with a "guilty man." He was dealing merely with the author of an injury, an irresponsible piece of fate. And the man on whom the punishment then fell like a piece of fate felt no more "inner pain" than he would feel at the sudden approach of some unforeseen event, some terrible natural catastrophe, a rushing, crushing avalanche against which there is no resistance.

15. This truth dawned insidiously on Spinoza (to the disgust of his commentators, who, like Kuno Fischer, for instance, go to endless trouble to misunderstand him on this point). One afternoon, as he sat raking up who knows what memory, he asked himself what was really left for him personally of the celebrated morsus conscientiæ. Here was a man who had relegated "good and evil" to the sphere of human imagination, and who indignantly defended the honor of his "free" God against the blasphemers who claimed that God did everything sub ratione boni ("but this was tantamount to subordinating God to fate, and would really be the greatest of all absurdities"). For Spinoza the world had gone back to that innocence in which it lay before the bad conscience was discovered. So what had become of the morsus conscientiæ? "The antithesis of gaudium," he said at last to himself: "A sadness accompanied by the recollection of a past event which has turned out contrary to all expectation" (Eth. III., Propos. XVIII. Schol. i. ii.). For thousands of years, evil-doers overtaken by punishment have felt about their "offence" exactly as Spinoza did: "here is something which went wrong contrary to my anticipation," not "I ought not to have done this." They submitted to punishment as one submits to a disease, a misfortune or death, with that stubborn, resigned fatalism that even now gives the Russians, for instance, an advantage over us Westerners in managing life. If actions were criticized at that period, the criterion was prudence. What punishment unquestionably achieves is chiefly a sharper sense of prudence, a longer memory, a will to be more cautious, suspicious and secretive from now on, a recognition that many things are unquestionably beyond one's capacity, and a kind of improvement in self-criticism. In man and beast alike, the broad results that punishment can obtain are increased fear, a sharper sense of cunning, and mastery of the desires. So punishment tames man, but does not make him "better"; it would be more correct even to go so far as to assert the contrary ("Injury makes a man cunning," says a popular proverb: so far as it makes him cunning, it makes him also bad. Fortunately, it often enough makes him stupid).

21. So much for my rough, preliminary sketch of how the ideas "ought" (owe) and "duty" are interrelated with the postulates of religion. Until now I have intentionally held back the actual moralization of these ideas (their being pushed back into the conscience, or more precisely the interweaving of the bad conscience with the idea of God). At the end of the last paragraph I spoke as if this moralization did not exist, and as if these ideas had therefore necessarily come to an end, since their hypothesis, the belief in our "creditor," in God, had collapsed. The actual facts differ terribly from this theory. With the moralization of the ideas "ought" and "duty," and their being pushed back into the bad conscience, comes the first actual attempt to reverse the direction of the development we have just described, or at any rate to arrest its progress. It is just at this juncture that the very hope of an eventual redemption has to shut itself once for all in the prison of pessimism; it is at this juncture that the eye has to recoil and rebound in despair from an adamantine impossibility; it is at this juncture that the ideas "guilt" and "duty" have to turn backwards. Turn backwards against whom? There is no doubt about it: primarily against the "ower." In him the bad conscience now establishes itself, eats, spreads and grows like a polypus throughout his length and breadth, and with such virulence that at last, with the impossibility of paying the debt, there is conceived the impossibility of paying the penalty, the thought of its inexpiability (the idea of "eternal punishment"). Finally it also turns against the "creditor." It may find him in the causa prima of man, the origin of the human race, its sire, who from then on is burdened with a curse ("Adam," "original sin," "determination of the will"). Or it may find him in Nature, from whose womb man springs, and on whom the responsibility for the principle of evil is now cast ("Diabolization of Nature"). Or it may find him in existence generally, which on this logic is an absolute white elephant, with which mankind is landed (the Nihilistic flight from life, the demand for Nothingness, or for the opposite of existence, for some other existence, Buddhism and the like). Then suddenly we stand before that paradoxical and awful expedient through which a tortured humanity found a temporary alleviation, that stroke of genius called Christianity: God personally sacrificing himself for the debt of man, God paying himself personally out of a pound of his own flesh, God as the one being who can deliver man from what man had become unable to deliver himself from — the creditor playing scapegoat for his debtor, from love (can you believe it?), from love of his debtor!...

Yet note that this Olympian spectator and judge is not at all angry with them, and does not think ill of them for it. "How foolish they are," he thinks of the misdeeds of mortals. And "folly," "imprudence," "a little brain disturbance," and nothing more, are what the Greeks, even of the strongest, bravest period, have admitted to be the ground of much that is evil and fatal. — Folly, not sin, do you understand?... But even this brain disturbance was a problem. "Come, how is it even possible? How could it really have got into brains like ours, the brains of men of aristocratic ancestry, of men of fortune, of men of good natural endowments, of men of the best society, of men of nobility and virtue?" This was the question the aristocratic Greek asked himself for century after century, whenever he was confronted with every (to him incomprehensible) outrage and sacrilege with which one of his peers had polluted himself. "It must be that a god had infatuated him," he would say at last, nodding his head. — This solution is typical of the Greeks, ... and accordingly the gods in those times served to justify man to a certain extent even in evil. In those days they took upon themselves not the punishment but, what is more noble, the guilt.

2. What do ascetic ideals mean? Or, to take one case on which I have often been consulted: what does it mean when an artist like Richard Wagner pays homage to chastity in his old age? In a certain sense he had always done so, of course. But only at the very end did he do it in an ascetic sense. What does this "change of attitude" mean, this radical revolution (for that is what it was)? Wagner swung right round into his own opposite. And what does it mean when an artist swings round into his own opposite? Here, if we are willing to dwell a little on the question, we think at once of the best, strongest, gayest and boldest period that Wagner's life perhaps ever had. It was the time when he was deeply and genuinely absorbed in the idea of "Luther's Wedding." Who knows by what chance we now have the Meistersingers in place of that wedding music? And how much of the one may be an echo of the other? Still, there is no doubt that the theme would have praised chastity. It would certainly have praised sensuality as well; and even so it would have seemed quite in order, and just as Wagnerian. For chastity and sensuality are not necessarily opposed: every good marriage, every authentic, heart-felt love, rises above that opposition. It seems to me that Wagner would have done well to bring this pleasing reality home to his Germans once more, with a bold and graceful "Luther Comedy." There were and are many revilers of sensuality among the Germans, and perhaps Luther's greatest merit is just that he had the courage of his sensuality (it used to be called, prettily enough, "evangelistic freedom "). Even where the opposition between chastity and sensuality really does exist, fortunately it has not needed to be a tragic one for some time now. That should hold for all beings sound in mind and body. They are far from counting their delicate balance between "animal" and "angel" as, on the face of it, one of the principles opposed to existence. The most subtle and brilliant spirits, Goethe and Hafiz for example, have even found in it a further charm of life. Such "conflicts" actually tempt one to live. On the other hand, it is only too clear what happens when these ruined swine are reduced to worshipping chastity (and there are such swine): all they see and worship in it is the opposite of themselves, the opposite of ruined swine. Oh, what tragic grunting and eagerness! Just imagine it. They worship that painful and superfluous contrast which Richard Wagner in his last years undoubtedly wanted to set to music and put on the stage! "For what purpose, forsooth?" we may fairly ask. What did the swine matter to him; what do they matter to us?

3. Here we cannot help asking what he really had to do with that manly (ah, so unmanly) country bumpkin, that poor devil and natural, Parsifal, whom he finally made a Catholic by such fraudulent devices. What? Was this Parsifal really meant seriously? One might be tempted to suppose the opposite, even to wish it: that the Wagnerian Parsifal was meant joyously, as the closing play of a trilogy or satyric drama, in which Wagner the tragedian wanted to take his leave of us, of himself, and above all of tragedy, in a fitting and worthy way. He would do it with an excess of the most extreme and flippant parody of the tragic itself, of the ghastly earthly seriousness and earthly woe of old; a parody of the crudest phase in the unnaturalness of the ascetic ideal, a phase long since overcome. As I have said, that would have been quite worthy of a great tragedian. Like every artist, he reaches the supreme peak of his greatness only when he can look down on himself and his art, when he can laugh at himself. Is Wagner's Parsifal his secret laugh of superiority at himself, the triumph of the supreme artistic freedom and artistic transcendency he has at last attained? We might, I repeat, wish it were so; for what can Parsifal amount to, taken seriously? Must we really see in it (in an expression once used against me) the product of an insane hate of knowledge, mind and flesh? A curse on flesh and spirit in one breath of hate? An apostasy and a relapse into the morbid Christian and obscurantist ideals? And, in the end, a self-negation and self-elimination by an artist who until then had put all the strength of his will into the opposite, the highest artistic expression of soul and body? Not only of his art, but of his life too. Remember how enthusiastically Wagner once followed in Feuerbach's footsteps. Feuerbach's motto of "healthy sensuality" rang in Wagner's ears in the thirties and forties of the century, as it did in the ears of many Germans (they called themselves "Young Germans"), like a word of redemption. Did he change his mind on this in the end? For at any rate it seems that in the end he wished to change his teaching on it ... and not only in the Parsifal trumpets on the stage. In the melancholy, cramped and embarrassed lucubrations of his later years, a hundred passages show a secret wish and will: a despondent, uncertain, unavowed will to preach actual retrogression, conversion, Christianity, mediævalism, and to tell his disciples, "All is vanity! Seek salvation elsewhere!" Even the "blood of the Redeemer" is invoked once.

6. Schopenhauer took over the Kantian treatment of the æsthetic problem, though he certainly did not look at it through Kantian eyes. Kant believed he was honoring art when he put in the foreground those predicates of the beautiful that make up the honor of knowledge: impersonality and universality. I will not discuss here whether this was a complete mistake. I only want to stress that Kant, like other philosophers, did not approach the æsthetic problem from the experiences of the artist (the creator). He considered art and beauty only from the spectator's standpoint, and so imperceptibly brought the spectator himself into the idea of the "beautiful"! If only the philosophers of the beautiful knew this "spectator" well enough! I mean knew him as a great fact of personality, as a great experience, as a wealth of strong and highly individual events, desires, surprises and raptures in the sphere of beauty! But, as I feared, the opposite was always the case. So from the very beginning our philosophers hand us definitions in which the lack of subtler personal experience squats like a fat worm of crass error. It does so in Kant's famous definition of the beautiful. "That is beautiful," says Kant, "which pleases without interesting." Without interesting! Set this definition beside another, made by a real "spectator" and "artist," Stendhal, who once called the beautiful une promesse de bonheur. Here the one point Kant stresses in the æsthetic position is rejected and struck out: le désintéressement. Who is right, Kant or Stendhal? Our æsthetes never tire of putting into the scales on Kant's side the fact that under the magic of beauty men can look at even naked female statues "without interest." Forsooth, we may laugh a little at their expense. On this ticklish point the experiences of artists are more "interesting," and at any rate Pygmalion was not necessarily an "unæsthetic man." Let us think all the better of the innocence of our æsthetes, mirrored in such arguments. Let us even count it to Kant's honor that he taught with such country-parson naïveté about the peculiar character of the sense of touch! And here we come back to Schopenhauer. He stood much closer to the arts than Kant did, and yet he never got outside the pale of the Kantian definition. How was that? The circumstance is marvelous enough. He reads the phrase "without interest" in the most personal way, out of an experience that in his case must have been part and parcel of his regular routine. On few subjects does Schopenhauer speak with such certainty as on the working of æsthetic contemplation. He says it simply counteracts sexual interest, like lupulin and camphor, and he never tires of praising this escape from the "Life-will" as the great advantage and utility of the æsthetic state. One is in fact tempted to ask whether his basic conception of Will and Idea, the thought that freedom from the "will" is possible only by means of "idea," did not originate in a generalization from this sexual experience. (In every question about the Schopenhauerian philosophy, one should, by the way, keep in mind that it is the conception of a youth of twenty-six. It shares, therefore, not only in what is peculiar to Schopenhauer's life but in what is peculiar to that special period of it.) Let us listen, for instance, to one of the most expressive of the countless passages he wrote in honor of the æsthetic state (World as Will and Idea, i. 231). Let us listen to the tone, the suffering, the happiness, the gratitude, in which such words are spoken: "This is the painless state which Epicurus praised as the highest good and as the state of the gods; we are during that moment freed from the vile pressure of the will, we celebrate the Sabbath of the will's hard labor, the wheel of Ixion stands still." What vehemence of language! What images of anguish and long-drawn revulsion! How nearly pathological is that temporal antithesis between "that moment" and everything else: the "wheel of Ixion," "the hard labor of the will," "the vile pressure of the will." But grant that Schopenhauer was a hundred times right for himself personally. How does that help our insight into the nature of the beautiful? Schopenhauer has described one effect of the beautiful, the calming of the will; but is this effect really normal? As was mentioned, Stendhal, a nature just as sensual but more happily made than Schopenhauer, points to another effect of the "beautiful." "The beautiful promises happiness." For him the essential fact seems to be precisely that beauty excites the "will" (the "interest"). And does Schopenhauer not finally expose himself to the objection that he is quite wrong to regard himself as a Kantian here? That he has altogether failed to understand the Kantian definition of the beautiful in a Kantian sense? That the beautiful pleased him too through an interest, in fact the strongest and most personal interest of all, that of the victim of torture who escapes from his torture? — And to return to our first question, "What does it mean when a philosopher pays homage to ascetic ideals?" Now we have, at any rate, a first hint: he wishes to escape from a torture.

7. Let us beware of pulling dismal faces at the word "torture." In this case there is certainly plenty to deduct and plenty to discount; there is even something to laugh at. For we must not underestimate the fact that Schopenhauer treated sexuality in practice as a personal enemy (including its tool, woman, that "instrumentum diaboli"), and that he needed enemies to keep him in good humor. He loved grim, bitter, blackish-green words. He raged for the sake of raging, out of passion. Without his enemies, without Hegel, woman, sensuality and the whole "will for existence," "keeping on," he would have fallen ill and become a pessimist (for he was not a pessimist, however much he wished to be). Without them Schopenhauer would not have "kept on"; that is a safe wager. He would have run away. But his enemies held him fast, and his enemies always lured him back to existence. His wrath was, as it was for the ancient Cynics, his balm, his recreation, his recompense, his remedium against disgust, his happiness. So much for what is most personal in Schopenhauer's case. On the other hand, much in him is also typical, and only now do we come back to our problem. It is an accepted and indisputable fact that, as long as there have been philosophers in the world, and wherever they have existed (from India to England, to take the opposite poles of philosophic ability), they have felt a real irritation and rancor towards sensuality. Schopenhauer is merely its most eloquent outburst and, for anyone with an ear for it, also the most fascinating and enchanting. Philosophers likewise have a real bias and affection for the whole ascetic ideal; let there be no illusions on this score. Both feelings, as has been said, belong to the type. A philosopher who lacks both is, you may be certain, never anything but a "pseudo." What does this mean? For this state of affairs must first be interpreted: in itself it stands there stupid, for all eternity, like any "Thing-in-itself." Every animal, la bête philosophe included, strives instinctively for an optimum of favorable conditions, in which it can let its whole strength play and attain its maximum feeling of power. With equal instinctiveness, and with a fine perceptive flair superior to any reason, every animal shudders mortally at every kind of disturbance and hindrance that blocks, or could block, its way to that optimum. (I am not talking about his way to happiness, but about his way to power, to action, to the most powerful action, and in fact in many cases his way to unhappiness.) In the same way the philosopher shudders mortally at marriage and at all that could persuade him to it, since marriage is a fatal hindrance on the way to the optimum. Which great philosophers have been married, up to now? Heracleitus, Plato, Descartes, Spinoza, Leibnitz, Kant, Schopenhauer: none was married, and, what is more, one cannot imagine them married. A married philosopher belongs to comedy. That is my rule. As for the exception, Socrates, the malicious Socrates seems to have married ironice, just to prove this very rule. Every philosopher would say what Buddha said when the birth of a son was announced to him: "Râhoula has been born to me, a fetter has been forged for me" (Râhoula means here "a little demon"). An hour of reflection must come to every "free spirit" (granted that an hour of thoughtlessness came first), just as it once came to that same Buddha: "Narrowly cramped," he reflected, "is life in the house; it is a place of uncleanness; freedom is found in leaving the house." Thinking so, he left the house. The ascetic ideal shows so many bridges to independence that the philosopher cannot help exulting and clapping his hands when he hears the story of all those resolute men who one day said nay to all servitude and went into some desert, even granting that they were only strong asses and the absolute opposite of strong minds. What, then, does the ascetic ideal mean in a philosopher? This is my answer, which will have been guessed long ago: when he sees this ideal, the philosopher smiles, because he sees in it an optimum of the conditions for the highest and boldest intellectuality. He does not thereby deny "existence." Rather he affirms his existence, and only his existence, and this perhaps to the point of being not far from the blasphemous wish, pereat mundus, fiat philosophia, fiat philosophus, fiam!

8. You see, these philosophers are far from being uncorrupted witnesses or judges of what the ascetic ideal is worth. They are thinking of themselves — what is the "saint" to them? What they have in mind is whatever they personally cannot do without: release from compulsion, disturbance and noise; release from business, duties and cares; a clear head; thoughts that dance, spring and fly; and good air — rare, clear, free and dry, the air of the heights, in which every animal creature grows more intellectual and sprouts wings. They have in mind peace in every cellar; every hound neatly chained; no baying of enmity, no uncouth rancor; no remorse from wounded ambition; internal organs that are quiet and submissive, busy as mills yet unnoticed; a heart that is alien, transcendent, future, posthumous. In short, what they mean by the ascetic ideal is the joyous asceticism of an animal that has been deified and newly fledged, and that sweeps over life instead of resting on it. The three great catch-words of the ascetic ideal are familiar to us: poverty, humility, chastity. Now look closely at the lives of all the great, fruitful, inventive spirits. Again and again you will find these three qualities in them, to a certain degree. This is, of course, not for a minute as though, perhaps, they belonged among such men's virtues — what has this type of man to do with virtues? — but because they are the most essential and natural conditions of such a man's best existence and finest fruitfulness. It is quite possible, in this connection, that their dominant intellectualism first had to rein in an unruly, irritable pride, or an insolent sensualism, or that it had its work cut out defending its wish for the "desert" against perhaps a leaning toward luxury and dilettantism, or against an extravagant generosity of heart and hand. Their intellect managed all this for one simple reason: it was the dominant instinct, and it imposed its orders on all the other instincts. It still does so; if it ceased, it would no longer be dominant. But in all this there is not one iota of "virtue." Further, take the desert I just mentioned, where the strong, independent and well-equipped spirits withdraw into their hermitage — oh, how unlike the desert the cultured classes dream of! In certain cases the cultured classes themselves are the desert. And it is certain that none of the actors of the intellect could endure that desert for even a minute. It is not romantic or Syrian enough for them; it is nowhere near enough of a stage desert! There are plenty of asses here too, but the resemblance stops there. A desert today looks more like this — perhaps a deliberate obscurity; stepping out of one's own way; a dread of noise, admiration, newspapers, influence; a little office, a daily task, something that conceals rather than reveals; at times the company of harmless, cheerful beasts and fowls whose sight refreshes; a mountain for company, though not a dead one, one with eyes (that is, with lakes); in some cases even a room in a crowded hotel, where one can count on going unrecognized and on talking with anyone without risk. That is the desert — oh, it is lonely enough, believe me! I admit that when Heracleitus withdrew to the courts and cloisters of the colossal temple of Artemis, his "wilderness" was worthier. Why do we lack such temples? (Perhaps we do not; I am thinking just now of my splendid study in the Piazza di San Marco, in spring, of course, and in the morning, between ten and twelve.) But what Heracleitus fled, we too avoid today: the noise and democratic babble of the Ephesians, their politics, their news from the "empire" (Persia, I mean, of course), their market-trade in "the things of today." For there is one thing above all that we philosophers need a rest from: the things of "today." We honor whatever is silent, cold, noble, far and past — in fact, anything the sight of which does not force the soul to brace and defend itself; something one can speak with without speaking aloud. Now listen to the tone of a spirit when it speaks; every spirit has a tone of its own and loves it. That one over there, for instance, is bound to be an agitator, that is, a hollow head, a hollow mug: whatever goes in comes back out of him dull and thick, heavy with the echo of the great void. That other spirit nearly always speaks hoarsely. Has he, perhaps, thought himself hoarse? It may be so — ask the physiologists. But someone who thinks in words thinks as a speaker and not as a thinker (this shows that he does not think about objects, or think objectively, but only about his relations to objects; in fact, that he thinks only of himself and his audience). A third speaks aggressively; he comes too near our body and his breath blows on us — we involuntarily shut our mouths, though he speaks to us through a book. The tone of his style supplies the reason: he has no time, he has little faith in himself, he finds expression now or never. A spirit who is sure of himself, however, speaks softly; he seeks secrecy and lets himself be waited for. A philosopher is recognized by his shunning three brilliant and noisy things, fame, princes and women — which is not to say that they do not come to him. He shuns every glaring light, and so he shuns his own time and its "daylight." In this he is like a shadow: the lower the sun sinks, the larger the shadow grows. As for his humility, he puts up with a certain dependence and obscurity just as he puts up with darkness. Further, he is afraid of the shock of lightning; he shudders at the insecurity of a tree that stands too isolated and exposed, on which every storm vents its temper and every temper its storm. His "maternal" instinct, his secret love for what is growing in him, leads him into states in which he is relieved of the need to look after himself, just as the "mother" instinct in woman has thoroughly preserved her dependent position down to the present. After all, they ask little enough, these philosophers; their favorite motto is, "He who possesses is possessed." As I must say again and again, none of this is to be put down to a virtue or to a meritorious wish for moderation and simplicity. It happens because their supreme lord demands it of them, wisely and inexorably — a lord who is eager for one thing only, and for that alone gathers and hoards everything: time, strength, love, interest. This kind of man does not like being disturbed by enmity, nor by friendship; it is a type that forgets or despises easily. He finds it bad form to play the martyr, to "suffer for truth"; he leaves that to the ambitious and the stage-heroes of the intellect, and to all those who have time for such luxuries (the philosophers themselves have something to do for truth). They use big words sparingly; they are said to dislike the very word "truth," which has a "high falutin'" ring.
