Finally, as for the chastity of philosophers: the fruitfulness of this type of mind lies plainly in another sphere than children; perhaps it is in some other sphere, too, that they have the survival of their name, their little immortality (philosophers in ancient India would say it with still greater boldness: "Of what use is posterity to him whose soul is the world?"). In this attitude there is no trace of chastity out of any ascetic scruple or hatred of the flesh, any more than it is chastity when an athlete or a jockey stays away from women. It is rather the will of the dominant instinct, at any rate during the time of their advanced philosophic pregnancy. Every artist knows how harmful sexual intercourse is in times of great mental strain and preparation. For the strongest artists, those with the surest instincts, this is not necessarily a matter of experience — hard experience; it is simply their "maternal" instinct, which, for the benefit of the growing work, recklessly spends the vigor of its animal life (beyond all its normal stocks and supplies). The greater power then absorbs the lesser. Now let us use this interpretation to judge correctly the case of Schopenhauer, already mentioned. In his case the sight of the beautiful evidently worked like a resolving irritant on the chief power of his nature (the power of contemplation and intense penetration), so that this strength exploded and suddenly became master of his consciousness. But that does not at all rule out the possibility that the particular sweetness and fullness peculiar to the æsthetic state springs directly from an ingredient of sensuality (just as the "idealism" peculiar to girls at puberty has the same source). It may be, then, that sensuality is not removed when the æsthetic state approaches, as Schopenhauer believed, but only transfigured, so that it no longer enters consciousness as sexual excitement. (I shall come back to this point in connection with the more delicate problems of the physiology of the æsthetic, a subject that has so far been singularly untouched and unelucidated.)

13. But let us turn back. The self-contradiction that seems to show itself among the ascetics, "Life turned against Life," is simply nonsense — this much is absolutely obvious — when judged from the physiological standpoint and not, now, the psychological one. It can only be an apparent contradiction. It has to be a kind of provisional expression, an explanation, a formula, an adjustment: a psychological misunderstanding of something whose real nature could not be grasped for a long time, and whose real essence could not be described. It is a mere word jammed into an old gap in human knowledge. Put briefly, the facts that count against its being real are these. The ascetic ideal comes out of the protective, self-preserving instincts of a decadent life, a life that tries by every means it has to hold its position and fight for its existence. It points to a partial physiological depression and exhaustion, and the deepest, still intact life-instincts keep fighting this ceaselessly with new weapons and new discoveries. The ascetic ideal is one such weapon. So its position is exactly the reverse of what its worshippers imagine: life is struggling in it and through it with death and against death, and the ascetic ideal is a dodge to keep life going. History teaches something important about how far this ideal could rule over man and exercise power over him, especially in every place where the civilization and taming of man was completed. What it shows is the diseased state of man up to now, at any rate of the tamed man: his physiological struggle with death (more precisely, with disgust with life, with exhaustion, with the wish for the "end"). The ascetic priest is the incarnate wish for an existence of another kind, on another plane. He is, in fact, the highest point of this wish, its official ecstasy and passion. Yet the very strength of this wish is the fetter that ties him down here. It is just this that turns him into a tool, one who has to labor to create more favorable conditions for earthly existence, for existence on the human plane. With this very strength he holds the whole herd of failures, distortions, abortions, unfortunates and sufferers from themselves of every kind fast to existence, while he walks instinctively ahead of them as their herdsman. You understand me already: this ascetic priest, this apparent enemy of life, this denier — he actually belongs among the really great conservative and affirmative forces of life.... Where does this diseased state come from? For man is more diseased, more uncertain, more changeable and more unstable than any other animal, there is no doubt of it — he is the diseased animal. So where does it spring from? Certainly he has also dared more, innovated more, braved more and challenged fate more than all the other animals put together. He is the great experimenter with himself, the unsatisfied, the insatiate, who fights for supreme mastery against beast, Nature and gods. He is the as yet ever uncompelled, the ever future, who can no longer find any rest from his own aggressive strength, driven mercilessly on by the spur of the future dug into the flesh of the present. How could so brave and rich an animal fail to be also the most endangered, the animal with the longest and deepest sickness among all sick animals?... Man grows sick of it, and often enough whole epidemics of this satiety break out (as around 1348, the time of the Dance of Death). Yet even this very nausea, this tiredness, this disgust with himself, is thrown off by him with such force that it is at once made into a new fetter. His "nay" to life brings forth, as though by magic, an abundance of graceful "yeas"; and even when he wounds himself, this master of destruction and of self-destruction, it is the wound itself afterward that forces him to live.

17. But is he really a physician, this ascetic priest? We already understand why we are scarcely allowed to call him one, however much he likes to feel like a "saviour" and to be worshipped as one. He combats only the actual suffering, the sufferer's discomfort, not its cause, not the actual state of sickness. This must be our most radical objection to priestly medication. Yet put yourself just once into that point of view, which the priests have a monopoly on, and you will find it hard to exhaust your amazement at all he has seen, sought and found from that standpoint. The mitigation of suffering, every kind of "consoling" — all this shows itself as his very genius. With what ingenuity has he interpreted his mission as consoler, with what aplomb and audacity has he chosen the weapons the part requires! Christianity in particular should be called a great treasure-chamber of ingenious consolations, so great a store of refreshing, soothing, deadening drugs has it piled up within itself. It has hazarded so many of the most dangerous and daring expedients; with such subtlety and refinement, Oriental refinement, it has divined which emotional stimulants can conquer, at least for a time, the deep depression, the leaden fatigue and the black melancholy of physiological cripples. For, speaking generally, all religions are mainly concerned with fighting a certain fatigue and heaviness that has infected everything. You can take it as prima facie probable that in certain places in the world there was almost bound to prevail from time to time, among large masses of the population, a sense of physiological depression. Owing to their lack of physiological knowledge, this did not appear to their consciousness as such, and so its "cause" and its cure could only be sought and tried in the science of moral psychology (this, in fact, is my most general formula for what is generally called a "religion"). Such a feeling of depression can have the most diverse origins. It may result from the crossing of too heterogeneous races (or of classes — genealogical and racial differences also show themselves in the classes: the European "Weltschmerz," the "Pessimism" of the nineteenth century, is really the result of an absurd and sudden class-mixture). It may be brought about by a mistaken emigration, a race falling into a climate for which its power of adaptation is insufficient (the case of the Indians in India). It may be the effect of old age and fatigue (the Parisian pessimism from 1850 onwards). It may come from a wrong diet (the alcoholism of the Middle Ages, the nonsense of vegetarianism — though these have in their favor the authority of Sir Christopher in Shakespeare). It may come from blood-deterioration, malaria, syphilis and the like (German depression after the Thirty Years' War, which infected half of Germany with evil diseases and thereby paved the way for German servility, for German pusillanimity). In such a case a war on a grand scale against the feeling of depression is invariably attempted. Let us inform ourselves briefly about its most important practices and phases (I leave aside, as stands to reason, the actual philosophic war against the feeling of depression, which is usually simultaneous — it is interesting enough, but too absurd, too practically negligible, too full of cobwebs, too much of a hole-and-corner affair, especially when pain is proved to be a mistake, on the naïf hypothesis that pain must needs vanish once the mistake underlying it is recognized — but behold! it does anything but vanish ...). That dominant depression is fought primarily by weapons that reduce the consciousness of life itself to the lowest degree. Wherever possible, no more wishes, no more wants; avoid everything that produces emotion, that produces "blood" (eating no salt, the fakir hygiene); no love; no hate; equanimity; no revenge; no getting rich; no work; begging; as far as possible, no woman, or as little woman as possible; as far as the intellect is concerned, Pascal's principle, "il faut s'abêtir." In ethical and psychological language, the result is "self-annihilation," "sanctification"; in physiological language, "hypnotism." It is the attempt to find some approximate human equivalent for what hibernation is for certain animals and æstivation for many tropical plants: a minimum of assimilation and metabolism in which life just manages to subsist without really entering the consciousness. An amazing amount of human energy has been devoted to this object — perhaps uselessly? There cannot be the slightest doubt that these sportsmen of "saintliness," of whom nearly every nation has at times had an abundance, really found a genuine relief from what they fought with such rigorous training. In countless cases they really did escape deep physiological depression with the help of their system of hypnotism, and their method is consequently counted among the most universal ethnological facts. Similarly it is improper to treat such a plan of starving the physical element and the desires as itself a symptom of insanity (as a clumsy species of roast-beef-eating "freethinkers" and Sir Christophers are fain to do). All the more certain is it that their method can and does pave the way to all kinds of mental disturbances, for instance "inner lights" (as with the Hesychasts of Mount Athos), auditory and visual hallucinations, voluptuous ecstasies and effervescences of sensualism (the history of St. Theresa). The explanation the victims give of such events is always the acme of fanatical falsehood; this is self-evident. Note well, however, the tone of implicit gratitude that rings in the very will to an explanation of such a character. They always regard the supreme state, salvation itself, that final goal of universal hypnosis and peace, as the mystery of mysteries, which even the most supreme symbols are inadequate to express. They regard it as an entry and homecoming to the essence of things, a liberation from all illusions, "knowledge," "truth," "being," an escape from every end, every wish, every action, something even beyond Good and Evil.

21. Where this kind of priestly medicine-mongering, the "guilty" kind, is concerned, every word of criticism is superfluous. As for the suggestion that emotional excess of this type, which in these cases the ascetic priest is eager to order for his sick patients (under the most sacred euphemism, as is obvious, and equally impregnated with the sanctity of his purpose), has ever really been of use to any sick man: who, if you please, would feel inclined to maintain such a proposition? At any rate, we should first come to an understanding about the expression "be of use." If you only mean that such a system of treatment has reformed man, I do not deny it. I merely add that to my mind "reformed" means as much as "tamed," "weakened," "discouraged," "refined," "daintified," "emasculated" (and so it means almost as much as injured). But when you are dealing mainly with sick, depressed and oppressed creatures, such a system, even granted that it makes the ill "better," always makes them more ill as well. Ask the mad-doctors what invariably results from a methodical application of penance-torture, contrition and salvation ecstasies. Ask history too. In every body politic where the ascetic priest has established this treatment of the sick, disease has each time spread with sinister speed through its whole length and breadth. What was always the "result"? A shattered nervous system on top of the existing malady, in the greatest as in the smallest, in individuals as in masses. The penance and redemption training gives us awful epileptic epidemics, the greatest known to history, such as the St. Vitus and St. John dances of the Middle Ages. Another phase of its after-effect is frightful mutilations and chronic depressions, which turn the temperament of a nation or a city (Geneva, Bale) once for all into its opposite. This training, again, is responsible for the witch-hysteria, a phenomenon analogous to somnambulism (eight great epidemic outbursts of this alone between 1564 and 1605). It also brings in its train those delirious death-cravings of large masses, whose awful "shriek," "evviva la morte!" was heard over the whole of Europe, interrupted now by voluptuous variations and now by a rage for destruction. Today the same emotional sequence, with the same intermittences and sudden changes, is observed universally wherever the ascetic doctrine of sin scores a great success once more (religious neurosis appears as a manifestation of the devil, there is no doubt of it. What is it? Quæritur). Speaking generally, the ascetic ideal and its sublime-moral cult, this most ingenious, reckless and perilous systematization of all methods of emotional excess, is written large in a dreadful and unforgettable fashion across the whole history of man, and unfortunately not only across history. I could scarcely name any other element that has done more destructive harm to the health and race efficiency of Europeans than this ideal. Without exaggeration, it can be called the real fatality in the history of the health of the European man. The most you can do is compare it with the specifically German influence: I mean the alcohol poisoning of Europe, which up to the present has kept pace exactly with the political and racial pre–dominance of the Germans (where they inoculated their blood, there too they inoculated their vice). Third in the series comes syphilis — magno sed proximo intervallo.

26. Or does the whole of modern history, perhaps, show more confidence in life and in its ideals? Its loftiest pretension today is to be a mirror. It rejects all teleology and wants no more "proving." It disdains to play the judge, and shows its good taste in that. It asserts as little as it denies; it fixes, it "describes." All this is ascetic to a high degree, yet nihilistic to a much higher degree; make no mistake about this! In the historian you see a gloomy, hard, but determined gaze, the eye of an isolated North Pole explorer (perhaps so as not to look within, so as not to look back?). There is snow; life is silenced here; the last crows that caw here are called "whither?", "Vanity," "Nada." Nothing more flourishes or grows here, except at most the metapolitics of St. Petersburg and the "pity" of Tolstoi. Then there is that other school of historians, a perhaps still more "modern" school, voluptuous and lascivious, which ogles life and the ascetic ideal with equal fervor, which wears the word "artist" like a glove, and has by now secured a "corner" for itself in all the praise of contemplation. Oh, what a thirst these sweet intellectuals arouse, even for ascetics and winter landscapes! Nay! The devil take these "contemplative" folk! I would much rather wander with those historical Nihilists through the gloomiest, grey, cold mist! Nay, I shall not mind listening (supposing I have to choose) to someone completely unhistorical and anti-historical (a man like Dühring, for instance, whose periods have intoxicated a hitherto shy and unavowed species of "beautiful souls" in contemporary Germany, the species anarchistica within the educated proletariate). The "contemplative" are a hundred times worse. Nothing has ever made me so intensely nauseous as one of those "objective" chairs, one of those scented mannikins-about-town of history, a thing half-priest, half-satyr (Renan parfum). The high, shrill falsetto of his applause betrays what he lacks and where he lacks it: it betrays where the Fates, in his case, have plied their ghastly shears, alas! in too surgeon-like a fashion! I find this distasteful, and it tries my patience. Let him stay patient at such sights who has nothing to lose by it. For me the sight is enraging; such spectators embitter me against the "play," even more than the play itself does (history itself, you understand). Anacreontic moods come over me imperceptibly. This Nature, who gave the steer its horn and the lion its χάσμ ὀδοντων: for what purpose did Nature give me my foot? — To kick, by St. Anacreon, and not merely to run away! To trample on all the worm-eaten "chairs," the cowardly contemplators, the lascivious eunuchs of history, the flirters with ascetic ideals, the righteous hypocrites of impotence! All reverence from me to the ascetic ideal, in so far as it is honorable! So long as it believes in itself and plays no pranks on us! But I do not like all these coquettish bugs, whose insatiable ambition is to smell of the infinite until at last the infinite smells of bugs. I do not like the whited sepulchres with their stagey imitation of life. I do not like the tired and the used up who wrap themselves in wisdom and look "objective." I do not like the agitators dressed up as heroes, who hide their dummy-heads behind the stalking-horse of an ideal. I do not like the ambitious artists who would fain play the ascetic and the priest, and are at bottom nothing but tragic clowns. I do not like, again, these newest speculators in idealism, the Anti-Semites, who roll their eyes in the patent Christian-Aryan-man-of-honor fashion today, and with moralist attitudes and agitation dodges so cheap that they exhaust any patience, try to rouse all the blockhead elements in the populace (the unfailing success of every kind of intellectual charlatanism in present-day Germany is tied to the almost indisputable and already quite palpable desolation of the German mind. I look for its cause in a too exclusive diet of papers, politics, beer and Wagnerian music, not forgetting the condition this diet presupposes: the national exclusiveness and vanity, the strong but narrow principle "Germany, Germany above everything," and finally the paralysis agitans of "modern ideas"). Europe today is above all wealthy and ingenious in means of excitement; it apparently has no more pressing need than stimulantia and alcohol. Hence the enormous counterfeiting of ideals, those most fiery spirits of the mind; hence also the repulsive, evil-smelling, perjured, pseudo-alcoholic air everywhere. I should like to know how many cargoes of imitation idealism, of hero-costumes and high-falutin' claptrap, how many casks of sweetened pity liqueur (Firm: la religion de la souffrance), how many crutches of righteous indignation to prop up these flat-footed intellects, how many comedians of the Christian moral ideal would have to be exported from Europe today before its air smelled pure again. It is obvious that this over-production opens up a new trade possibility, and obvious that a new business is to be done in little ideal idols and obedient "idealists" — don't pass over this tip! Who has the courage? We hold in our hands the possibility of idealizing the whole earth. But what am I saying, courage? Here we need only one thing — a hand, a free, a very free hand.
